content: Primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more from the genital tract within 24 hours after childbirth. It is a leading cause of maternal mortality globally and contributes to significant physical and psychological complications. This review focuses on the effectiveness and safety of mechanical and surgical interventions for managing primary PPH. The review included nine small randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 944 women from various countries, including Pakistan, Turkey, Thailand, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Benin, and Mali. The overall quality of evidence was very low to low, primarily due to study design limitations, imprecision, and indirectness. Many important outcomes were not reported, and the heterogeneity of the studies prevented meta-analysis. External Uterine Compression vs. Normal Care One trial involving 64 women provided very low-certainty evidence, making it unclear whether external uterine compression affects the need for blood transfusion (risk ratio [RR] 2.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66 to 8.23). Uterine Artery Embolization vs. Surgical Devascularization Plus B-Lynch Suture A single trial with 23 women provided very low-certainty evidence, leaving the effect on hysterectomy rates (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.15 to 3.57) and intervention side effects (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.08 to 15.41) unclear. Intrauterine Tamponade Various methods of intrauterine tamponade were studied, including the Bakri balloon, condom-loaded latex catheter, latex balloon catheter, and traditional gauze packing. 1. Balloon Tamponade vs. Normal Care One study (116 women) using a condom catheter suggested it may increase blood loss of 1000 mL or more (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.00), but the evidence was of very low certainty. Other outcomes, such as mortality due to bleeding (RR 6.21, 95% CI 0.77 to 49.98), hysterectomy (RR 4.14, 95% CI 0.48 to 35.93), total blood transfusion (RR 1.49, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.51), and side effects, were also unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Another study (240 women) using a latex balloon catheter with cervical cerclage provided very low-certainty evidence, leaving the effects on hysterectomy (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.74) and additional surgical interventions (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.12) unclear. 2. Bakri Balloon Tamponade vs. Hemostatic Square Suturing A small trial (13 women) found no mortality, serious maternal morbidity, or side effects. The effect on blood transfusion was unclear (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.14 to 2.36). Bakri balloon tamponade may reduce mean intraoperative blood loss (mean difference [MD] -426 mL, 95% CI -631.28 to -220.72), but the evidence was of very low certainty. 3. Comparison of Intrauterine Tamponade Methods One study (66 women) compared the Bakri balloon and condom catheter, but it was uncertain whether the Bakri balloon reduces the risk of hysterectomy (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.05 to 5.25) or blood transfusion (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.06) due to very low-certainty evidence. Another study (50 women) compared the Bakri balloon with and without a traction stitch, but the effect on hysterectomy (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.97) was unclear. A third study (212 women) compared the condom catheter to gauze packing and found that the condom catheter may reduce fever (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.59), but the evidence was of very low certainty. Modified B-Lynch Compression Suture vs. Standard B-Lynch Compression Suture One trial involving 160 women provided low-certainty evidence suggesting that a modified B-Lynch compression suture may reduce the risk of hysterectomy (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.99) and postoperative blood loss (MD -244.00 mL, 95% CI -295.25 to -192.75). Authors' Conclusions There is insufficient evidence from RCTs to determine the relative effectiveness and safety of mechanical and surgical interventions for treating primary PPH. High-quality randomized trials are urgently needed, and new emergency consent pathways should facilitate recruitment. The finding that intrauterine tamponade may increase total blood loss >1000 mL suggests that introducing condom-balloon tamponade in low-resource settings without broader quality improvement measures may not reduce PPH-related deaths or morbidity. The potential superiority of the modified B-Lynch suture over the original technique requires further investigation before widespread adoption. In high-resource settings, uterine artery embolization is increasingly used, but its efficacy remains under-researched. Future trials should adopt standardized PPH core outcomes to improve consistency and enable meta-analyses.
